extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners evaluating §101 patent-eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the two-part Alice/Mayo patent-eligibility test (Step 2A prong two and Step 2B) including the 'particular treatment or prophylaxis' consideration and the search for an inventive concept. Focused on how to determine when additional claim elements integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular treatment and prophylaxis (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; one way to demonstrate such integration is when the additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such application or use meaningfully limits the claim by going beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment. Claims qualifying under this consideration are eligible at Step 2A because they are not 'directed to' the recited judicial exception. Examples include administration steps that treat or prevent a disease (e.g., administering a drug in a dose range depending on genotype).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment/prophylaxis limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of affirmative limitations: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient.' Mere intended use, a field-of-use limitation, or a recitation that a product is a 'pharmaceutical composition' are not affirmative treatment/prophylaxis limitations. A step of 'prescribing' is not positive if it does not require actual use by/on the patient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity (specificity) of the treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular,' i.e., specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a specific administration step (e.g., 'administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker to a patient identified as having the poor metabolizer genotype') which integrates the exception, with a generic instruction ('administering a suitable medication to a patient') which is not particular and thus does not integrate the abstract idea. Examiners may evaluate this alongside 'mere instructions to apply' and 'field of use and technological environment' considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: More-than-nominal relationship to the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed treatment meaningfully relates to the recited law/correlation (e.g., administering insulin to reduce risk of ketoacidosis linked to high blood glucose is meaningfully related; administering aspirin in that context is at best nominal). Consider also the 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and 'field of use' considerations when determining meaningful relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation must not be merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits and cannot be extra-solution activity or mere field-of-use instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an administration step is performed only to gather data (a necessary precursor) it is extra-solution activity and does not integrate the judicial exception. Conversely, an applying step that uses analysis results to alter treatment and lower risk integrates the abstract idea into a practical application. See examples contrasting data-gathering vaccine administration vs applying a lowest-risk vaccination schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (Step 2B): additional elements must amount to 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'inventive concept' is furnished by an element or combination of elements that is recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception, and is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself. Evaluating additional elements requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure they amount to significantly more than the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating whether additional elements amount to an inventive concept requires considering claim elements both individually and as an ordered combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because claims must be 'considered as a whole,' an element that is not sufficient on its own may nonetheless supply an inventive concept when combined with other elements (e.g., non-conventional arrangement of known components in BASCOM; combination of freezing/thawing steps in CellzDirect). Follow the example in Alice: identify additional elements, consider each individually (are they well-understood, routine, conventional?), then consider the ordered combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for an inventive concept is distinct from novelty/obviousness (§102/§103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept should not be confused with a novelty (§102) or non-obviousness (§103) determination; novelty of an element is of no relevance to whether a claim falls within §101 categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of novelty or obviousness does not necessarily indicate that additional elements are routine/conventional, and conversely patentability under §§102/103 is neither required for nor a guarantee of §101 eligibility. Do not substitute §§102/103/112 inquiries for the §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations that can indicate 'significantly more' (illustrative list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has identified several non-exclusive considerations relevant to whether additional elements amount to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of limitations courts have found to qualify as 'significantly more' include: (i) improvements to the functioning of a computer; (ii) improvements to any other technology or technical field; (iii) applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine; (iv) effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; (v) adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment (e.g., immunization step integrating data comparison into a process that lowers disease risk). The list is not exclusive and elements may be analyzed under more than one consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that courts have found insufficient to supply 'significantly more' (illustrative list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of additions to a claim are generally not enough to qualify as significantly more than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of insufficient limitations: (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; (ii) appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality (generic computer functions); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering; (iv) generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. See MPEP §2106.05(f)-(h) for examples and case citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/tangibility of additional elements is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element(s) is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B; tangible implementation alone does not guarantee an inventive concept, nor does intangibility doom eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A computer is a tangible machine, but reciting a generic computer to implement an abstract idea does not make the claim patent-eligible (Alice). Conversely, improvements that are not defined by physical components may still be eligible (Enfish; McRO). Consult case law examples where physical steps did not supply an inventive concept and where non-physical improvements did.

rubrics_metrics.name: How courts conduct the 'significantly more' analysis (Alice and BASCOM examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court practice: identify additional elements, consider each element individually for whether it is well-understood, routine, conventional, and then consider the elements as an ordered combination to determine whether the combination supplies an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice: Court identified additional computer functions and hardware, found each to be generic and well-understood, and concluded the ordered combination added nothing significant. BASCOM: district court identified elements as well-known generic components but failed to consider whether their unconventional, non-generic arrangement (installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable features) constituted an inventive concept. Use specification evidence when appropriate to assess conventionality and consider combination.
